title: ‘Please can I have one more picture’: the US airmen accused of child sexual abuse in UK who avoided British trial
summary:
Guardian investigation reveals US military personnel, including ‘multi-child molester’, convicted in courts martial

When Jacob Ozbirn, an American airman, drove to a country lane near a…
byline: Rob Evans, Harry Davies, Louisa Loveluck and Emine Sinmaz

blocks.text: When Jacob Ozbirn, an American airman, drove to a country lane near a Derbyshire hotel one summer’s evening, he was expecting to meet a 12-year-old girl he had been grooming for sex.
In the previous days, he had sent explicit messages to her and two other girls, encouraging them to send him naked photos, despite having been told by all three that they were aged 12 or 13.
In one message, he wrote: “There is nothing to be afraid of. I will take care of you! And please can I have one more picture.”

Ozbirn drove two hours from RAF Mildenhall, the huge US airbase in Suffolk where he was stationed, to meet one of them near Burton upon Trent. But he had walked into a sting run by “paedophile hunters”, members of the public who pose online as girls to lure suspected paedophiles to meetings where they confront them.
Ozbirn told the paedophile hunters he was simply seeking to educate the girls about dangerous predators, but they notified Derbyshire police who detained him.

Ozbirn should have been investigated by the local police force and, if necessary, prosecuted in a British criminal court. Instead, Derbyshire police handed over the investigation to the US military police. He was brought before a court martial, held on the Mildenhall base, and sent to a US military jail for three years.
The Guardian has now identified at least 21 American airmen in the UK who have been convicted of child sexual abuse offences in the last decade. Only three were prosecuted in UK courts.

The rest were brought in front of US courts martial, which, critics argue, provide a more limited form of justice. Juries, sometimes all-male, are made up of the defendant’s peers. Unlike hearing in the open British courts, members of the public are unable to easily attend courts martial held on US airbases.
Accounts of these proceedings are often too sparse to determine whether UK police have, or should have, been involved.
Documents relating to courts martial are published on a public register in an inconsistent way, often disappearing with no explanation. Charges are described in a limited way or not at all.

Rachel VanLandingham, a retired lieutenant colonel and former military lawyer, said that for decades the transparency of the US military justice system had been “woefully inadequate”. “It’s been brought to the military’s attention time after time again,” she said. “It’s intentionally opaque. They want it to be opaque.”
US requests

There are more than 12,000 US military personnel working on at least 15 bases and facilities across the UK. Under an official agreement dating back to the 1950s, any US military personnel accused of breaking the law should be investigated by a British police force unless the alleged offences are committed while on duty or against another member of the US armed forces, its property, or a dependant such as a spouse or child.

But the Guardian has uncovered a growing number of cases in which UK police forces have acquiesced to requests by the US military to take control of investigations into potential wrongdoing by members of the American armed forces.
The agreement is now the subject of a high-level internal inquiry examining whether US military personnel stationed in Britain are being prosecuted properly.

The inquiry, which involves at least four Whitehall departments and police chiefs, was set up after the Guardian revealed in June how UK police had permitted the US military to take over an investigation into an American pilot who strangled a British woman in his flat in Cambridge.

The pilot, Jacob Wulfson, was instead tried in a US court martial that was held on his base at RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk. Downing Street said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson.

blocks.caption: Jacob Wulfson. Photograph: Tech Sgt Joseph Pick/US Air Forces Central

blocks.text: The US military uses courts martial to prosecute its personnel for a range of types of offences such as sexual violence against women, assaults, drug-taking and failing to obey orders.

An analysis shows that out of the 63 military personnel who have been convicted at courts martial in the UK going back to 2016, 18 have been convicted of child sexual abuse offences – more than a quarter of the total.
The offences include the rape and sexual abuse of children under the age of 12 and acquiring large amounts of child pornography.
Most recently, two airmen were convicted in October in separate courts martial that took place on the Lakenheath base.

The first airman was sentenced to 10 years in a military jail for sexually abusing a child and possessing and obtaining child pornography. He is known only as Lucero, as the US military has not published his first name.
William Berroa was sent to a military jail for two years for possessing and viewing child abuse images. The US air force has published no details of their offending.
The Guardian asked the US air force military police, the Office of Special Investigations (OSI), if it had asked the British police to take over jurisdiction for the investigation of these cases.

The OSI did not answer this question. In a statement, it said: “As in all our investigations, the Air Force Office of Special Investigations worked with our UK partners to determine investigative primacy.

“Extensive negotiations took place to establish jurisdiction. While we cannot give details, these were decisions that were not made quickly or spuriously. Ultimately, the local authorities have the right of first refusal on all investigative matters.”
A UK refusal

The US military wants to handle as many of the prosecutions of its personnel as possible. The Americans frequently ask to take over investigations from UK police forces, even when it appears clear that they would fall within the responsibility of the British authorities. Many times the UK police agree. But sometimes they refuse.

One such instance involved Jarik Lofthus, an airman at Mildenhall. In 2025, British police raided his home in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, and seized pornographic images of young children and bestiality.
Suffolk police said they rejected a request from the US military to take over the case. The US air force did not respond when asked for a comment.
In July, Lofthus, 33, was sentenced at Ipswich crown court to eight months in jail, suspended for two years.

In another case, Sam Jarvis, 36, was convicted in June of sexually assaulting a 12-year-old girl at a social event in Oxfordshire. At Oxford crown court, Jarvis, who was stationed at the American base at RAF Croughton in Northamptonshire, was given an 18-month jail sentence, suspended for two years.

The US air force declined to say whether it had sought to take over the investigation into Jarvis. It said: “Criminal jurisdiction for this case was determined consistent with the status of forces agreement.”
It added that it “works in close coordination with local UK law enforcement agencies and respects the authority of UK court proceedings”.

Thames Valley police, who investigated Jarvis, said they could not say whether the US military had asked to take over jurisdiction, referring questions to the Americans. “Thames Valley police is not able to comment on behalf of partner agencies,” the force added.
Low conviction rate

Among the 18 cases dealt with by the US military, the longest sentence was handed to Brandon Justice, a US air force technical sergeant who was described by military investigators as a “multi-child molester”. Following a court martial at Lakenheath in 2016, he was sentenced to 47 years in a military jail.
A sentence of 30 years in a military jail was given to Christopher Toolan, a staff sergeant, at a Lakenheath court martial in 2024.

Over four years, he had committed multiple offences. He had noted on his phone how he had raped a child under the age of 12, adding: “I was in heaven.” He was also convicted of sexually abusing another and possessing images of child abuse.

The court martial heard how late one evening he had approached a girl who was playing in a park at Lakenheath and showed her photograph of a girl, aged six or seven, who was laying naked on a red blanket.
Garret Souders, a technical sergeant at Mildenhall, was convicted after his wife discovered his sexual fantasies about raping, torturing and killing their four young daughters.

On New Year’s Day in 2019, she checked his phone and found graphic exchanges with other men on a website in which he described his “darkest fantasies” of “handing his very young children over to a group of men to use however they wanted”.

His court martial heard how he imagined other men raping his daughters, and when they did, it was always “hard and rough and violent, and sometimes they don’t survive”. He was jailed for nine years in 2021.
However, there is concern that the US air force is not doing enough to tackle paedophiles within its ranks.

Don Christensen, a retired colonel, spent 23 years working in the US military justice system. He was a judge, a prosecutor and a defence lawyer in many courts martial. In recent years, he has been involved in moves to reform the US military justice system.

He said that in his experience there was a low conviction rate for child sexual abuse offences. He attributed this partly to the intrinsic nature of the US military justice system, in which juries consist of fellow members of the armed forces.

He said: “A lot of times, there is a natural tendency for military members to believe that other military members, the people they serve with, whether they know this person or not – you know, we’re still like the band of brothers – that they would [not] do something as horrific as child sex offences.”

He also said there was disincentive for relatives to report an airman for, for example, the rape of his daughter, since the family would then be at a financial disadvantage if he was convicted and dismissed from the US military.

A US air force spokesperson said: “There is no place in our ranks or in our communities for anyone who exploits or abuses a child. The United States Air Force is committed to the investigation and prosecution of anyone accused of these offenses and to maintaining good order and discipline within our forces.”
